product_scope: Lose It! Snap It is a Premium photo-logging feature that returns detected foods and estimated serving sizes for user review and editing.
supported_platforms: Mobile iOS and Android product; current public support documentation describes a mobile photo workflow. A current APK was not locally analyzed in this pass.
pricing: Snap It is Premium-only. Lose It does not publish a separate developer/API price for Snap It. Source: https://loseit.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/47771695186580-How-to-Use-Snap-It
popularity_signal: Google's historical case study says Lose It had helped more than 30 million people by the time of publication; this is platform scale, not current Snap It usage. Source: https://developers.google.com/ml-kit/case-studies/lose-it
recognition_behavior: The current support flow is photo/upload -> detected foods and estimated serving size -> user can edit, swap, or add items. Clear and bright photos improve results.
identified_services: [uncertain] Current Snap It provider/model is not disclosed. Google published a historical case study describing a custom Snap It model deployed with ML Kit and compressed/quantized TensorFlow Lite; that is strong historical evidence for the 2019-era implementation, not confirmation of the current app.
model_or_provider_confidence: [uncertain] Historical ML Kit/TFLite attribution is high-confidence for the cited case study; present-day architecture and model version are unknown.
local_inference_evidence: Google's case study explicitly says Snap It moved from a GPU server to a quantized custom model running on-device, including offline real-time inference, with models hostable/updated through Firebase. Current behavior was not re-confirmed.
portion_and_nutrition_method: The product exposes estimated serving size and maps the selected food to Lose It nutrition records; user editing is part of the workflow. No current public evidence shows measurement-grade portion or calorie estimation.
artifact_source: No current official APK was locally decompiled for this item. Public package indexes were used only to identify the Android package boundary; no runtime testing was performed.
static_findings: Historical official Google documentation is the strongest technical evidence: compressed/quantized TFLite custom model, ML Kit on-device deployment, Firebase model delivery, and offline real-time behavior. This is a documented product case study rather than fresh binary proof.
reverse_engineering_limits: The historical case study cannot establish current model versions, cloud fallbacks, data retention, or feature flags. No current APK installation or traffic inspection was attempted.
candidate_models: A compact food detector/classifier in Core ML or LiteRT is the closest local analogue. Use local inference for fast candidates and a cloud fallback for ambiguous multi-food or recipe cases.
mobile_runtime_support: ML Kit/LiteRT is a natural Android path; Core ML is the native iOS equivalent. ONNX Runtime Mobile is a cross-platform alternative.
device_requirements: Quantized small models can support broad device coverage; updateable model delivery is useful for drift but requires versioning, rollback, and privacy controls.
expected_food_inference_quality: On-device latency/offline behavior is achievable, but food taxonomy drift and complex meals remain risks. Evaluate missed foods, top-k recall, serving error, and correction time rather than speed alone.
unit_cost_estimate: A local model has no per-photo cloud charge; engineering, downloads, battery, and support are the main costs. Any current Lose It unit cost is not public.
privacy_and_compliance: Historical on-device inference reduces image transfer for that path. If a cloud fallback exists today, the app must disclose it separately; do not infer privacy behavior from the historical case study.
recommendation: Use the historical Snap It pattern as evidence that a small quantized local food model is viable for fast candidate generation, then measure a modern hybrid fallback on current devices.
